title: Examine the teacher
hookLine: the Buddha invites monks to investigate even him

lines: A BOSS WHO SAYS: CHECK ME.
cards: A new boss, on your first day, says: here's how to tell whether I'm honest. Watch what I do when I think nobody's looking. Watch whether fame changes me.
Ask me hard questions, and see if my answers hold. Then decide how far to trust me. That's roughly what the Buddha did.
He gave his monks a method for investigating him.

teach.b: This is the forty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the inquirer.
A monk who can't read another person's mind, the Buddha says, should examine the Tathagata, the Buddha himself, to find out whether he is truly awakened. Then he gives the method.
Watch with your eyes, listen with your ears. Is there anything defiled in him? Anything mixed, sometimes clean and sometimes not?
Or only what is clean? Has he had these good qualities a long time, or only recently?
Has fame changed him? Some teachers are fine until they become well known, and then dangers appear. Is he restrained because he's free of desire, or only because he's afraid?
And then, ask him directly. A teacher worth trusting will say: my conduct is clean, and that is my path, but I don't identify with it.

teach.h: FAITH WITH REASONS CAN'T BE SHAKEN
teach.b: Faith built like this, the Buddha says, rooted in reasons, is firm. No ascetic or brahmin, no god, no Mara, no Brahma, no one in the world can shake it. That's the twist.
He isn't asking for less faith.
He's asking for faith that's been checked, with roots of its own, and the teacher welcomes the scrutiny. It isn't cynical.
Watching a teacher's conduct over time, in fame and in private, is what turns admiration into trust.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes cite MN 47, alongside the Kalama Sutta, when encouraging students to examine teachers and teachings over time before placing trust in them; in Tibetan Buddhism, students are traditionally advised to examine a teacher carefully before accepting them.

o: a doubter who refuses every teacher
an inquirer who checks a teacher with care
a student who never questions a teacher

games.q: the inquirer's questions — tap the pairs.
p: watch and listen to his conduct
firm; no one can shake it

s: the Buddha told monks to accept him without question
he gave them a method for investigating whether he was truly awakened.
MN 47 asks whether fame has changed the teacher
some teachers are fine until they become well known; the inquirer checks for that.
investigating the teacher is meant to weaken faith
the Buddha says faith built on reasons is firm, and no one can shake it.

games.q: you're a new monk. you can't read minds. how does the Buddha say you should find out whether he is truly awakened?
o: watch and listen over time, then ask him directly.
games.why: the method is patient observation of conduct, in private and in fame, and then direct questions. faith that grows that way is rooted.

practice: Think of someone whose advice you follow, a teacher, a writer, a coach, a parent, a voice online, and run the Buddha's questions gently: what do I actually see them do, is it clean or mixed, has attention changed them?
Don't rush to a verdict; there's nothing disloyal in looking. Then let the questions go and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Vimamsaka. The inquirer: the Buddha's own method for checking him, by eye, ear, time and fame, so that faith rests on reasons.

orig.note: Pali vimamsaka: an inquirer, one who investigates. the discourse is the Vimamsaka Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: investigate the teacher. Checked faith has roots of its own. Until next time.
